catalog_quote: There are some vowels in the data which are not included in Figure 7. The vowels [o ŏ] are probably allophones of /əu əŭ/, occurring in unstressed syllables or shortened by a glottal stop. There are a few cases where [a ă] likewise seem to be shortened forms of an open -> close diphthong, and [i] seems to be a shortened or unstressed pronunciation of /ei/ or /i/. ... Phonation, tone, and glottalization act in concert in Padaung, making it difficult to know a priori which of the features is contrastive. Padaung has three tones: high falling [42], mid [3], and low tones [2] and [1]. Tone [1] is always closed with a glottal stop in utterance final position. Tone [3] can optionally be closed with a glottal stop. Phonation can occur on the mid [3] and low tone which I have labelled [2]. Breathy vowels are not closed with a glottal stop.

new_statements.rule_in_words: Padaung (Kayan) is described as a tone language (3-4 tones interacting with phonation and final glottal stop); the only reference to stress is that reduced vowels [ɐ ə] occur in unstressed syllables (i.e. there are unstressed, reduced syllables alongside full tonal syllables). The source gives no rule for where word stress falls; by implication the pattern is the Karenic sesquisyllabic one (reduced toneless presyllable + full final syllable), which Manson 2009 states only as an areal generalisation ('sesquisyllabic (i.e. they have iambic stress)'), not for Kayan specifically.
new_statements.exceptions: None; Kauffman flags his Padaung tone/phonation analysis as untested ('I have not tested which of those features, if any, is contrastive').
new_statements.domain_note: Based on a 406-item wordlist elicited mostly in isolation (citation forms) from one speaker (Lapi, c. 40, farmer from Demoso, NW Kayah State) recorded in Thailand; a 5-page synchronic sketch inside a comparative-tonal MA thesis, not a full phonology. The authoritative descriptions (Manson 2007, 2010) were not accessible.
new_statements.identity_note: All material located concerns the Pekon/Demoso 'Padaung' = Kayan Lahwi [pdu], kaya1315: Manson's 2007/2010 works describe the Pekon (Phekhon) dialect, the standard variety (Glottolog language code 'Pekon = Kayan [pdu]'); Kauffman 1993's 'Padaung' speaker is from Demoso, NW Kayah State; Luangthongkum's 'Kayan' is from Huai Suea Thao, Mae Hong Son (Padaung refugee community). Ywar 2013 (downloaded) is Kayan Lahta (Lahta-Zayein cluster, zaye1235/kxk), a different, mutually unintelligible language, and must not be used for kaya1315. Shintani's many 'X Kayan' LSTCA doculects are village-named and their assignment to pdu vs. Yinbaw/Gekho/Lahta could not be verified.

tone_statements.quote: With regard to Central Karen, synchronically, Kayan and E. Kayah have four tones in the non-checked syllable and two tones in the checked one like Pa-O. However, the patterns of tone split and merger differ. It is also noticeable that the mid-falling tone in Kayan and E. Kayah which may be regarded as the fifth tone rarely occurs and when it does, more often than not, the words turn out to be Burmese or Shan loanwords. ... In Kayan, E. Kayah, Bwe and Kayaw, the *A tone has split into two tones, i.e. A12-3, and there is no split in the *B tone column.
tone_statements.locator: p. 89, right column (tone discussion just before/around the heading 'Proto-tones and their development'); Kayan tone values in Appendix Table 1 'Correspondence patterns of the tones', p. 108
tone_statements.summary: Kayan: 4 non-checked + 2 checked tones per the author; Table 1 (p. 108): *A1/A2 > 53, *A3 > 33, *B > 11, *D1/D2 > 45’, *D3 > 21’ (’ = CVʔ). A rare mid-falling tone is called a possible 'fifth tone', so the author's total (5 or 6) is ambiguous; 60+ pitch-numbered Kayan forms. No TBU or stress claim.

tone_statements.quote: 6.5 Tones / There are four contrastive tones in Padaung / Phonemic Notation | Description | Tone stick | Phonetic Transcription / /1/ a mid-level tone [33] / /2/ a low-falling tone [21] ~ [31], [..21] / /3/ a high-falling tone [52] / /4/ a high-rising tone [45], [..45] / Table 9 : Padaung Tones ... /1/ represents [33], a mid-level tone. tone_statements.locator: pp. 72-73, sec. 6.5 Tones and Table 9 'Padaung Tones', sec. 6.5.1; also abstract 'four tonemes: mid level tone, low-falling tone, high-falling tone and high-rising tone'
tone_statements.summary: Four tonemes (mid level 33, low falling 21~31, high falling 52, high rising 45) on major and minor syllables; presyllables have neutralized mid pitch; tones 2, 4 have breathy allotones; minimal pairs in 6.5.2; auditory fieldwork, acoustic study left for future work. Stress predictable, word-final.

sources.note: Classifies the Kayan languages by the fate of Shintani's proto-tone 1-bis: in Mon-Khmer-influenced Kayan (Phaikhun group) proto-tone 1-bis merged with proto-tone 1; in Tay-influenced Kayan (Thandaung group and Loikaw-Dimoso group) it merged with proto-tone 3; Burmese-influenced Kayan (Pinmana group) developed nasalized vowels. Keywords: tone 1-bis, phantom tone. Tone-box based comparative classification drawing on his 1990s-2020s LSTCA Kayan doculects.

sources.quote: 6.5 Tones / There are four contrastive tones in Padaung / Phonemic Notation | Description | Tone stick | Phonetic Transcription / /1/ a mid-level tone [33] / /2/ a low-falling tone [21] ~ [31], [..21] / /3/ a high-falling tone [52] / /4/ a high-rising tone [45], [..45] / Table 9 : Padaung Tones ... /1/ represents [33], a mid-level tone. The pitch pattern of this tone starts at mid-level pitch and goes on the same range. ... /2/ represents [21] ~ [31] and [..21], a low-falling tone. ... It has two allotones ... [..21] a low falling tone accompanied with breathiness.
sources.locator: pp. 72-73, sec. 6.5 Tones and Table 9 'Padaung Tones', sec. 6.5.1; also abstract 'four tonemes: mid level tone, low-falling tone, high-falling tone and high-rising tone'
sources.note: Four tonemes (mid level 33, low falling 21~31, high falling 52, high rising 45) on major and minor syllables; presyllables have neutralized mid pitch; tones 2, 4 have breathy allotones; minimal pairs in 6.5.2; auditory fieldwork, acoustic study left for future work. Stress predictable, word-final.
